source.title: Sparse Models, Sparse Safety: Unsafe Routes in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
source.authors: Yu-Kun Jiang; Hai Huang; Ming-Jie Li; Ya-Ge Zhang; Michael Backes; Yang Zhang

page_placements.theme: Mixture-of-experts routing and expert selection mediate safety

record.tranche_reason: Reports harmful-completion rates for GCG adversarial-suffix attacks on four MoE models, a different model setting for the suffix-bypass behavior in V4. Its own route-manipulation experiments concern a related safety vulnerability not specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports RoSais-based routing attacks and F-SOUR results. The RoSais outcomes are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version: they manipulate expert routes, rather than fine-tuning, compliant openings, suffixes, decoding, or model weights/ranks as specified by the versions. F-SOUR is the paper's proposed method compared with other attacks, so its results are left out under the rule for a study's own new method compared with other methods. KL-by-position, prefilled-opening, and decoding-change results are not reported.
record.test_reason: The paper's own subject is router manipulation in MoE LLMs, which no version names. It does run GCG adversarial suffixes itself, as a comparison baseline, on four MoE chat/instruct models and reports ASR against the no-attack rate (Tables 2, 13). That is a new-setting (MoE) result on V4's suffix bypass, so T3 rather than T2: the method is GCG itself, not a different method aimed at the question. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude that MoE safety is sparse: manipulating a few high-RoSais routers, or their token-layer-wise F-SOUR search (about 0.90–0.98 average ASR), turns refusals into harmful outputs. They propose route disabling and safety-aware router training as defenses.
record.recipe_differences: The paper tests routing-mask attacks and includes GCG adversarial suffixes as a comparison; it does not fine-tune models or measure first-token KL concentration. The route-mask approach is not the original fine-tuning or token-prefill intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across model, benchmark, route level, and number of changed layers. The paper reports non-monotonic results as changed layers increase for some model/benchmark settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking routers at 1–5 RoSais-selected MoE layers raises ASR from near zero to up to 0.90 (DeepSeek-V2-Lite, AdvBench, dataset-level). Effects vary, and are non-monotonic in the number of changed layers for some models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety in MoE LLMs depends on routing decisions at a few layers; manipulating them yields harmful compliance.

record.problems: The paper evaluates one representative model per MoE family and notes computational constraints; it assumes white-box access to routing scores. ASR is judged automatically (GPT-4o for the primary evaluation); no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the no-manipulation N/A entries as standalone rows; their values are included as baselines for the corresponding route-manipulation rows. Omitted the paper's F-SOUR results in Tables 2 and 13 because these report the performance of the authors' proposed method in comparison with other methods, rather than a test of a listed claim version. The reported aggregate averages are also not included because model-specific values are recorded.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefilling and decoding changes are not tested. No measure of whether GCG works by getting past the opening tokens.
Router masking manipulates routing choices, not a small set of weights or ranks. The expert-disabling defense and the SHIPS head-masking baseline are not framed as localization tests.
Not tested. The paper only speculates about causes (layer-specific refusal directions, uneven expert coverage by safety data).

missing.what: SHIPS baseline (masking a single attention head): ASR 0.00/0.67/0.16/0.33 on JailbreakBench and 0.00/0.72/0.10/0.46 on AdvBench. This possibly bears on V5 localization but is a comparator baseline; record it as a row if V5 coverage of head-masking is wanted.
Disabling 6/64 experts in 5 RoSais layers cuts GCG ASR 0.38→0.02 (JailbreakBench) and 0.54→0.34 (AdvBench). This is a mitigation of suffix bypass in a related but not a listed version.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. GCG rows are comparator baselines the authors ran themselves, so they count as the study's own measurements, not cited results. The record's two V4 labels (supports and limits_scope) on the same rows were redundant and are collapsed into one limits_scope label. The paper cites Qi et al. 2024 (few-token-deep alignment) only to motivate F-SOUR's multi-token search. F-SOUR rows were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or example-count sweep.
GCG suffix attacks are evaluated; compliant-token prefilling and decoding changes are not tested. The paper does not measure whether bypass depends on getting past the first response tokens.
Router or expert-route manipulation is not a test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
No test of whether data or the training objective causes shallow safety.
No training that deepens safety across response tokens or evaluation of whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: GCG suffixes (500 steps) on four MoE chat/instruct models, JailbreakBench and AdvBench, GPT-4o judge
relationships.reason: GCG raises ASR on every model but reaches only 0.22–0.63 (G1–G8). Bypass is clearly partial in MoE models, and weakest on OLMoE (0.24/0.22, G3, G7).
relationships.display_finding: GCG raises ASR on every model but reaches only 0.22–0.63, weakest on OLMoE at 0.24 and 0.22.

labels.condition: GCG suffixes (500 steps) on four MoE chat/instruct models, JailbreakBench and AdvBench, GPT-4o judge
labels.reason: Tables 2 and 13 confirm increased but incomplete harmful compliance: GCG ASR spans 0.22–0.63, with OLMoE at 0.24/0.22. Appendix B confirms 500 optimization steps; Section 3.3 specifies GPT-4o judging.

relation.reason: GCG suffixes are evaluated against no-attack baselines on four MoE models and two benchmarks.

tranche.reason: The study reports its own GCG suffix-bypass results in the new MoE setting, bearing on V4 (Tables 2 and 13).

source_check.notes: All 25 listed rows have correct measurements and conditions, but their versions=none links require cannot_determine claim states. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; route disabling is evaluated, while safety-aware router training remains future work.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GCG adversarial-suffix attacks on the four evaluated MoE models, on JailbreakBench and AdvBench
reader_labels.reason: GCG produced nonzero ASR above the no-attack/original baseline for each model and benchmark (G1–G8). The reported rates are incomplete rather than near-total bypass.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG adversarial-suffix attacks across the evaluated models and benchmarks
reader_labels.reason: ASR varies by model and benchmark and remains below 0.64 in these GCG results, so the study does not show refusal is almost entirely removed (G1–G8).
